sweep_summary: maor1244 is not in the catalog. Six Glottolog title hits, none with an open copy: Philippson 1988 (Études océan indien 9, print-only; covers 'all Comorian dialects' but on Anjouan data per Lafon), Philippson 2005 (Tervuren, print-only; the one item with explicit first-hand Shimaore prosody, known only through Patin's quotations of pp. 212-213: phrase-level pitch accent, residual lexical marked/unmarked contrast in short phrases, default penultimate foot in longer phrases, antepenult tone at utterance level), Jouannet 1989 (Shingazidja; read via Lafon's 1991 review), Ahmed-Chamanga 1986 and Jaffar 1992 (both Anjouan/Ndzwani, print-only or unlocatable), and Philippson 1991 (thesis read in full from the author-posted PDF: Comorian = purely accentual, treated only through Ndzuani, obligatory penultimate feet, no Shimaore data). HAL and OpenEdition are behind Anubis by automated download. Best first-hand Shimaore statement remains Rombi 1983: 61-62 (page images re-read this search of works with stress in the title): stress on the penultimate syllable, shifting with locative/extension suffixes and prefixes, realised by pitch, with tone vestigial (p. 63). Acquisition priorities: Philippson 2005 (high), Philippson 1988 (high), Madi 2005 Lyon 2 thesis full text (not a title hit but claims 'accent libre'; server unreachable). Everything with and updated.

new_statements.quote: 1.3. L'ACCENT TONIQUE. Il se manifeste par la hauteur vocalique et par une articulation plus ferme. a) les polysyllabiques. L'accent tombe sur l'avant-dernière syllabe, exemples : 'da-go "village", dzi-'vu-zi "plume", 'nyu-mba "maison". L'adjonction d'un locatif ou d'une extension verbale entraîne un déplacement de l'accent tonique vers la droite, exemples : 'nyu-mba "maison" / nyu-'mba-ni "dans la maison" ; 'a-mba "dire" / a-'mbi-a "dire à". b) les monosyllabiques. new_statements.translation: 1.3. WORD STRESS (accent tonique). It is manifested by vowel pitch and a firmer articulation. a) polysyllables: stress falls on the penultimate syllable, e.g. 'da-go 'village', dzi-'vu-zi 'feather', 'nyu-mba 'house'. Adding a locative or a verbal extension shifts the stress to the right: 'nyu-mba 'house' / nyu-'mba-ni 'in the house'; 'a-mba 'say' / a-'mbi-a 'say to'. b) monosyllables: they are stressed. Adding a prefix shifts the stress to the left: 'ji 'voice' (sg.), 'ma-ji 'voices' (pl.).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (a pitch-plus-articulatory prominence) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, and it re-computes when suffixes/prefixes are added, so the penult of the derived word carries it (nyumba > nyumbáni; ji > máji). Monosyllables are stressed. All syllables are open (§1.4), so no weight sensitivity is at stake.
new_statements.exceptions: Rombi §1.5 (pp. 62-64): Comorian tone is 'vestigial en shimaore'; a small minority of the youngest informants keep tonal oppositions, lexical (maži 'water' vs mažÍ 'voice' cl.6; tsi 'eyebrow' vs tsÍ 'country') and grammatical (EPD vs copula, ligari lÁdagoni vs ligari la dagoni; accomplished tsisómó vs habitual negative tsisómo); older speakers give the impression of a tone language but analysis was impossible on the corpus; p. 64: 'n'a été vérifié.. qu'avec deux informateurs sur six'. Later work disputes the plain penult rule: Madi 2005 (abstract only) says Shimaore is 'à accent libre alors que le swahili est à accent fixe'; Philippson 2005: 212-213, as quoted by Patin 2018/2022, keeps tone patterns on short phrases (ɓawá dziɗu 'black wing' vs ɓawa pána 'broad wing') and derives a left-dominant binary foot over the last two syllables (final extrametrical) only for phonological phrases of more than two tone domains, with 'one tone on the antepenult' at utterance level (riudzu maʒwai máili). Treat Rombi's rule as the default/citation-form pattern with a residual lexical accent contrast.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (nouns, verbs, monosyllables with and without affixes); Rombi separates phrase-level intonemes (interrogation, insistence) in §1.5 and calls the word accent 'démarcatif de mot'. Description of Shimaore of Mayotte from Mahorais (and Mozambique-resident Mahorais) informants; Rombi & Alexandre-style INALCO Bantu framework.
new_statements.identity_note: Rombi 1983 describes Shimaore of Mayotte = maor1244 exactly (Glottolog names: Maore Comorian / Shimaore / Mahorais). Sibling varieties held by the project are ngaz1238 (Shingazidja) and mwal1237 (Shimwali); the Patin papers and Lafon review used here are primarily about Shingazidja and only quote Philippson 2005 on Shimaore second-hand. Rombi's informants were Mahorais (some resident in Mozambique); she notes (p. 64) that her tone observations rest on 2 of 6 informants, and calls tone 'vestigial' in Shimaore versus better preserved in Shimwali/Shindzuani.

new_statements.translation: 1.3 Word stress. It is manifested by vowel pitch and by a firmer articulation. a) Polysyllables: stress falls on the penultimate syllable, e.g. 'dago 'village', dzi'vuzi 'feather', 'nyumba 'house'. Adding a locative or a verbal extension shifts the stress one syllable to the right: 'nyumba 'house' / nyu'mbani 'in the house'; 'amba 'say' / a'mbia 'say to'. b) Monosyllables are stressed. Adding a prefix shifts the stress to the left: 'ji 'voice' (sg.) / 'maji 'voices' (pl.).

new_statements.reading: First-hand description of Shimaore (Mayotte) with fixed, weight-insensitive penultimate word stress realised chiefly by pitch; the shift examples show it is computed on the derived word (locative -ni, extensions, prefixes). Rombi p. 63 adds that Shimaore's suprasegmental system is 'très proche de celui du swahili : accent démarcatif de mot' and that lexical tone is vestigial (kept only by a minority of informants; verified with two of six informants, p. 64). This is the only first-hand Shimaore stress statement read in this search of works with stress in the title. Caveats to record alongside it: Philippson 2005: 212-213 (unobtained, quoted by Patin) analyses Shimaore as a phrase-level pitch accent system with a residual lexical marked/unmarked contrast in short phrases (ɓawá dziɗu vs ɓawa pána) and a default penultimate foot in longer ones; Madi 2005 (thesis abstract only, full text unreachable) calls Shimaore 'à accent libre'. A catalog entry should code fixed penultimate as the word-level default while flagging the residual-tone/phrasal overlay.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Abstract only: Shimaore is an accent (stress) language like Swahili, but with free (non-fixed) accent placement, in contrast to Swahili's fixed (penultimate) accent. No placement rule, no examples and no page numbers are available from the abstract; the 768-page thesis (five chapters, one on prosody) presumably gives the analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: All three listed works are about Shimaore (Mayotte) or Comorian generally: Alnet 2009 and Madi 2005 are explicitly on Shimaore/the parler of Mayotte; Philippson 1988 covers 'le comorien' and, per Lafon 1991, its rules are stated for Ndzwani (Anjouan) and Ngazidja, not Shimaore. Rombi 1983 (catalog source) is Mayotte Shimaore. Philippson 1991 (held by the project, not in the works list) treats Comorian through Ndzwani only and has no Shimaore data.

readall_conflicts: The only first-hand Shimaore description actually read (Rombi 1983, already in the catalog, §1.3 pp. 61-62) states fixed penultimate word stress computed on the derived word, with lexical tone vestigial. Madi 2005, the largest description of Shimaore (768 pp.), says in its abstract that Shimaore is accentual like Swahili but 'à accent libre' (free accent), explicitly opposed to Swahili's fixed accent; this contradicts the catalog's fixed: penultimate syllable type, but only the abstract could be opened (the Lyon 2 full-text server times out), so no placement rule, page or example is available. Philippson 1988 (not obtained; known through Lafon 1991) analyses Comorian accent as metrical with lexically/morphologically marked syllables, on Ndzwani and Ngazidja data, and Philippson 2005 (per Patin, noted in the existing statements) treats Shimaore as a phrase-level pitch accent system with a residual lexical marked/unmarked contrast and a default penultimate foot. Alnet 2009 remains login-restricted. So the sources split between a fixed: penultimate syllable default (Rombi 1983; Philippson 2005's default foot) and a lexically marked / free accent analysis (Madi 2005 abstract; Philippson 1988 by report)
